title: Writing Task 2: Opinion Essay
topic: Menulis esai opini dengan posisi, alasan, dan pertimbangan yang jelas
objectives: Menyatakan posisi (standpoint) dengan jelas di awal esai
Membenarkan posisi dengan alasan yang masuk akal

block1.tip: Esai opini yang baik menyatakan posisi di awal, membenarkannya dengan alasan, lalu menimbang keberatan sebelum menutup dengan kesimpulan yang kuat.

youtube.videoDescription: Video 10 sampai 15 menit tentang struktur esai opini, dari posisi awal sampai pertimbangan keberatan.
watchFor: Posisi yang jelas di paragraf pertama

lesson.intro: Esai opini meminta kamu menyatakan posisi tentang sebuah isu, lalu membenarkannya. Kekuatan esai ini ada pada alasan yang jelas dan sikap yang adil terhadap pandangan yang berbeda.

sections.heading: Posisi
sections.bodyMd: Nyatakan **standpoint** dengan jelas di awal. Jika kamu yakin, tunjukkan **conviction** melalui kata yang tegas, tanpa berlebihan.

sections.heading: Alasan
sections.bodyMd: Setiap alasan perlu **rationale** yang jelas. Gunakan contoh untuk **justify** posisimu. Sumber yang kamu pakai harus **credible**.

sections.heading: Keberatan
sections.bodyMd: Akui bahwa isu ini **debatable**, lalu **weigh** kedua sisi. Keberatan yang dijelaskan dengan adil membuat esaimu lebih **persuasive** dan **reasonable**.

block3.title: Esai Opini: Pekerjaan Rumah untuk Anak Kecil
block3.text:
Should schools limit homework for young children? My standpoint is clear: they should. This essay will justify that position using three points, and it will weigh the main objections fairly.

The first argument is about rest. Children who work for hours after school have less time to play, sleep, and relax. Many teachers would agree that a tired child learns less during the day. This is a reasonable concern, and it is not limited to one country. The rationale is simple: learning needs energy, and energy needs rest.

The second argument concerns family life. When homework fills every evening, parents become teachers instead of guardians. Arguments about tasks can damage the relationship between a child and a parent. A short, focused assignment can support learning without turning the home into a second classroom.

Critics offer a strong contention. They argue that homework builds discipline, and that without it children will struggle later. This is a debatable claim, and I accept that some practice helps. However, the research that is most credible suggests that quality matters more than quantity. Ten focused minutes can be more useful than an hour of repeated exercises.

The third argument is about fairness. Children from homes with quiet study spaces and internet access can finish tasks quickly. Others cannot. A heavy workload therefore widens the gap between students, even when they have equal ability. Limiting the amount of homework reduces that unfair advantage.

My conviction grows from these points, but I do not claim the issue is simple. Some children enjoy extra practice, and some families want more structure. A school policy should therefore allow teachers to set optional tasks for those who want them.

In the end, the aim of education is to build curiosity, not fatigue. A policy that protects rest, family time, and fairness is persuasive because it serves the whole child. It is a view that many parents, teachers, and students can accept. Schools that adopt such a policy can also review it each year, using feedback from families and pupils to decide whether the limit should be adjusted. This kind of open review shows that the school is willing to listen, which makes the policy more credible and easier to defend.
